[MUJAHID:v1p327#2/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | The rain fills each valley to the amount it can hold.
[MUJAHID:v1p327#2/r2] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | The foam is the froth carried along by the flood.
[MUJAHID:v1p327#2/r3] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | The sought-after metal goods are iron, copper, and lead.
[MUJAHID:v1p327#2/r4] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | The metalworking foam is the dross, corresponding to flood foam; it goes away as sediment, while the beneficial water remains on earth, illustrating truth and falsehood.
[MUQATIL:13:17-18/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The parable contrasts disbelief and faith, truth and falsehood: rainwater represents the Quran taught to believers and abandoned by disbelievers; valleys carry water according to their size.
[MUQATIL:13:17-18/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The flood carries foam that rises high.
[MUQATIL:13:17-18/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The jewelry sought from fire is gold and silver; utensils and goods include brass, iron, and lead, which also produce foam when heated.
[MUQATIL:13:17-18/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Foam from the flood is useless, and heating jewelry or goods expels the useless impurities while the useful metals remain.
[MUQATIL:13:17-18/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Water represents Quranic truth, valleys hearts, and the flood desires; useful water and purified metal represent truth that benefits its people in the Hereafter, while foam and slag represent useless falsehood.
[MUQATIL:13:17-18/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Jufāʾ means dried up and useless, like foam that benefits people not at all.
[MUQATIL:13:17-18/r7] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Useful water remains for drinking and irrigation, just as useful truth remains and benefits its people; God sets forth likenesses in these three examples together.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإشباعفيالجروالرفعوغيرالإشباعوالحركةكماهي)#745/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some speakers lengthen kasra and damma into ياء and واو; others clip the vowels quickly while retaining their movement.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإشباعفيالجروالرفعوغيرالإشباعوالحركةكماهي)#745/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The vowel is still mobile in the clipped pronunciation, as shown by speakers clearly articulating the ن in من مأمنك; a silent consonant would not allow that.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإشباعفيالجروالرفعوغيرالإشباعوالحركةكماهي)#745/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | This clipping does not occur in the accusative because fatḥa is lighter; its vowel measure remains, as with a hamza pronounced between full and elided forms.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإشباعفيالجروالرفعوغيرالإشباعوالحركةكماهي)#745/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poets may suppress a nominative or genitive vowel by analogy with dialectal shortening in فخذ and عضد; the cited line shows the practice.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإشباعفيالجروالرفعوغيرالإشباعوالحركةكماهي)#745/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The rajaz line is understood as صاحبي, with the final vowel shortened in verse; the poet's informants confirmed that intended form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإشباعفيالجروالرفعوغيرالإشباعوالحركةكماهي)#745/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Sibawayh cites a line by Imru al-Qays on ishmaam, a partial rounding of the vowel, which the manuscript marks with a dot.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإشباعفيالجروالرفعوغيرالإشباعوالحركةكماهي)#745/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The ishmaam pattern does not occur in the accusative, just as speakers who shorten كبد and فخذ do not use the analogous form for جمل.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصرففيالمذكرالبتةمماليسفيآخرهحرفالتأنيث)#534/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A masculine name of three letters without a feminine marker is fully declinable, except when its form is verb-like or begins with a verbal augment; the short masculine pattern readily bears nunation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصرففيالمذكرالبتةمماليسفيآخرهحرفالتأنيث)#534/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Names such as قدما and حشا remain declinable when diminutized: diminutive formation is light and no shorter pattern is available.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصرففيالمذكرالبتةمماليسفيآخرهحرفالتأنيث)#534/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A diptote takes genitive case when annexed or when preceded by the definite article, since these contexts remove the need for nunation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصرففيالمذكرالبتةمماليسفيآخرهحرفالتأنيث)#534/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Masculine names based on بنت or أخت are declinable because their ت is part of the built name, unlike the feminine هاء; the ت behaves like that in عفريت.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصرففيالمذكرالبتةمماليسفيآخرهحرفالتأنيث)#534/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A name derived from هنت becomes هنة with the ن moved and هاء retained; the rare form follows the regular pattern once made a proper name.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصرففيالمذكرالبتةمماليسفيآخرهحرفالتأنيث)#534/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A name from ضربت becomes ضربة: four consecutive vowels are avoided, so the final ت is treated as feminine هاء.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After verbs such as ظننت and وددت, أن and its clause occupy a noun phrase slot, as though the speaker said ذاك.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In إن لك هذا علي وأنك لا تؤذي, the second أن may attach to the first clause or begin independently; the cited Quranic phrase also has two readings. | mentions 20:119
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An open أن clause is a verbal noun and does not normally follow إن or another أن directly; the sequence is avoided because it resembles competing governed nouns and clauses.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | لم أنه ظريف is expanded as an implied question and answer: قلت لمه, ثم قلت لأن ذاك كذلك.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After أي, closed إني begins a clause meaning أنا نجد, while open أني is causal, meaning لأني نجد.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After لو or لولا, أن clauses function like ذا; Sibawayh illustrates the construction with a Quranic example and a line of poetry. | mentions 17:100
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ما رأيته مذ أن الله خلقني, أن occupies a noun slot equivalent to ذاك after مذ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil analyzes open أن after أما as an emphatic assertion, equivalent to حقا أنه منطلق.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil analyzes أما إنه as an alertive expression equivalent to ألا إنه ذاهب.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After أما والله, open أنه conveys an assertion that the speaker knows it, while closed إنه is alertive, like ألا إنه والله.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After ثم, open أن remains governed by the first عرفت, while closed إن starts a new statement and is no longer governed by it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمنأبوابأن)#498/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After رأيته شابا, closed إنه starts an independent clause; open وإنه is possible when the clause is attached to the verb, as in the cited poetry.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The accusative noun after مني can be a locative, meaning the person is in a place relative to the speaker; expressions with بمنزلة الولد make this ظرف sense clear.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The cited poet raises the second place phrase as equivalent to the first; the construction likens the speaker's place to a tick's place on a camel.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In دارى خلف دارك فرسخا, the accusative measure clarifies the vague distance after a complete predicate, like the specification after عشرون درهما.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yunus reports Abu Amr's stronger analysis دارى من خلف دارك فرسخان, treating خلف as a noun; Sibawayh says Arabs also parse خلف as a predicate and use either case.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أنت مني فرسخين can be ظرف, meaning that the distance holds while the two people travel for two farsakhs.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A time noun is accusative as a ظرف when an event occurs in it, as in القتال يوم الجمعة and الهلال الليلة; reversing order does not change that parse, while raising makes the latter noun identical with the first.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Day names such as الأحد and الاثنين must be raised as omitted ordinal descriptions; dates like اليوم خمسة عشر من الشهر likewise mean the day completes that number.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In اليوم يومك, the first اليوم means now rather than a specific day; عهدى به قريبا or حديثا is accusative when it means recently, but raised when the second noun identifies the first.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In عهدى به قائما and علمى به ذا مال, the accusatives are circumstantial predicates, not time adverbs; the same applies to ضربى عبد الله قائما.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Time expressions are especially noun-like because th

ey can serve as agents or patients, as in أهلكك الليل والنهار and استوفيت أيامك.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Abu Dhu'ayb's مقعد رابئ الضرباء is a place expression, located behind the star, and supports the locative construction.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Al-Ahwas uses مناط الثريا as a locative expression for the place where the Pleiades are suspended.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | These place nouns can omit في, as in دخلت البيت and ذهبت الشأم, but this ellipsis is restricted to expressions attested in Arabic and cannot be freely used with any noun.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | درج السيل means the place where the flood ran; Ibn Hurma's درج السيول illustrates the expression, and رجع أدراجه means retracing one's route.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Rafʿ with distances, lengths of travel, and time spans states the interval between two people; فوت اليد emphasizes how close they are.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | مرأى ومسمع is raised because it is treated as a noun for a specific place and as equivalent to the first predicate, not as a ظرف.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Sibawayh reports that some unnamed speakers use accusative مرأى ومسمع, treating it like درج السيول; this is a less common analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولالعربسمعناهمنهمهومنىمنزلةالشغافوهومنىمنزلةالولد|#196/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yunus reports some speakers treating مزجر الكلب, مقعد, and مناط like مرأى ومسمع, as nouns equivalent to the first predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاعبداللهحقاوهذازيدالحقلاالباطلوهذازيدغبرما#175/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil says لا قولك is accusative like لا ما تقول: it stands in the slot of a relative clause and distinguishes this statement from what the addressee says.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاعبداللهحقاوهذازيدالحقلاالباطلوهذازيدغبرما#175/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In the question أجدك لا تفعل, أجدك means أحقا, from الجد; the fixed expression retains its genitive annexation like لبيك and معاذ الله.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاعبداللهحقاوهذازيدالحقلاالباطلوهذازيدغبرما#175/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | غير ما تقول is annexed to a known expression to reinforce the prior statement; bare غير قول would not specify which saying is meant, while غير قيل باطل is clear.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكهذاعبداللهحقاوهذازيدالحقلاالباطلوهذازيدغبرما#175/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | البتة is only used definite; جهدك and أجهدك require annexation, whereas الحق and الباطل can be definite or indefinite because they remain fully inflected nouns like الظن and اليقين.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكماكانمنالمقاديروذلكقولكمافيالسماءموضعكفسحاباولى#281/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With a measure expression such as موضع كف, a partitive من is omitted before the measured material; the following accusative states its quantity or extent.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكماكانمنالمقاديروذلكقولكمافيالسماءموضعكفسحاباولى#281/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil treats the genitive after the measure word as a substitute for nunation; like a tanwin it leaves the measure indefinite, and the accusative then specifies its kind.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكماكانمنالمقاديروذلكقولكمافيالسماءموضعكفسحاباولى#281/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After ملء الدار, the specification may be singular or plural; the plural is allowed as with كم when it carries a collective sense like رب.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكماكانمنالمقاديروذلكقولكمافيالسماءموضعكفسحاباولى#281/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The line by Ka'b ibn Ju'ayl puts مرفدا in the accusative as a specification of the preceding number, illustrating the measured-noun construction.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكماكانمنالمقاديروذلكقولكمافيالسماءموضعكفسحاباولى#281/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | لا كزيد فارسا is understood with an omitted noun, as though it said لا فارس كزيد فارسا, with the final accusative specifying the comparison.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكماكانمنالمقاديروذلكقولكمافيالسماءموضعكفسحاباولى#281/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | تالله رجلا is elliptical for تالله ما رأيت كاليوم رجلا or وما رأيت مثله رجلا.
[FARRA:v2p60/r8] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The rainwater is a parable for the Qurʾan descending to people: hearts receive it according to their capacities and inclinations.
[FARRA:v2p62/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The useless foam represents what remains in the heart of an unbeliever who worships idols and is left with nothing; what benefits people and remains on earth represents the believer.
[FARRA:v2p62/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | When gold, silver, and copper are heated, the impurity extracted is foam like that on a torrent; jewelry and useful wares are what people seek from the metals.
[FARRA:v2p62/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The metals are heated to obtain ornaments or useful goods such as copper and iron; their scum is the corresponding foam.
[FARRA:v2p62/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | جفاء is long in form and derives from جفأ الوادي غثاءه جفئا, when a valley sweeps away its scum; it is like غثاء and other collective mass nouns, can function as a noun, and denotes what disappears quickly.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#45/r7] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Some read sūra with hamza and others without; the unhamzated form means a station or rank, as al-Nābigha's verse depicts honor above kings.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#45/r8] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The Qur'anic plural is suwar with open wāw in both reading traditions, while a building's plural is sūr with wāw at rest; he cites al-ʿAjjāj for the latter.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r10] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | He lists constructions where singular wording refers to a plural and plural wording refers to a dual.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r11] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Other number patterns include plural reports expressed as singular and a plural used as singular when paired with another singular.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r12] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | For two or more referents, a sentence may give the predicate to a singular or plural form and omit the report about the others.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r13] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | He lists a construction that assigns the predicate of two or more referents to the first.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r14] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | He also lists a construction that assigns the predicate of two or more referents to the last.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r15] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | He includes forms that use human-style reporting for animals and inanimate things, and treats animals as the nonhuman beasts.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r16] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Arabic may address an absent referent while meaning the present one.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r17] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Arabic may address the present and then switch the address to an absent form.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r18] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | A letter may be added in the wording while the intended construction is understood by dropping it.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r19] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | An implicit element can be left unexpressed when context makes it unnecessary to state.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r20] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Repetition can serve emphasis, while concise phrasing can dispense with repeated wording.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r21] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Arabic permits fronting and delaying elements, as well as assigning a predicate to something related to its original subject.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r22] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Abu ʿUbayda concludes that all these figures occur in accepted Arabic speech.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Abu ʿUbayda insists that the Qur'an was revealed in clear Arabic and rejects the claim that it contains non-Arabic words.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | rejects | He rejects the claim that Ṭā Hā is Nabataean, identifying it instead as an opening expression and a name and emblem of the sura. | mentions 20:1
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r5] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Similar-sounding words can share a meaning across Arabic and Persian without proving foreign origin; he compares Arabic istabraq/Persian istabra and Persian kūz/Arabic jawz.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r6] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | rejects | He rejects deriving sijjīl from Persian sang wa-gil and says the word means something hard or strong. | mentions 105:4
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r8] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The Qur'an contains the rare vocabulary and meanings found in Arabic speech.
[MAJAZ:v1p17/r9] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Among Arabic rhetorical devices in the Qur'an are abbreviation, deletion, and withholding a predicate or report.
[MAJAZ:v1p328/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Rābiyan is the active participle of rabā yarbū, meaning swelling or rising.
[MAJAZ:v1p328/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Matāʿ means what one enjoys or uses; al-Mushaʿath’s verse calls something that outlasts death matāʿ.
[MAJAZ:v1p328/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The phrase means God sets forth the truth and sets forth falsehood.
[MAJAZ:v1p328/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abū ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlāʾ says ajfaʾat al-qidr describes a pot whose scum spills out as it boils, or whose scum disappears when it settles.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p334#2/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says each valley carries water according to its capacity: the large according to its size, and the small according to its size.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p334#2/r2] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says foam rises above the water; similarly, when gold is heated, its pure part remains and its dross

 disappears, illustrating truth against falsehood.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p334#2/r3] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says foam clings to trees and comes to nothing, representing falsehood; what benefits people remains in the earth and produces fruit, representing truth.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p334#2/r4] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda identifies the metal goods as brass and iron.
[IBNHISHAM:v2p338#2/r1] IBNHISHAM, d. 213 · أبو هريرة | reports | On the return from Khaybar, a slave gifted to the Prophet by Rifa'a ibn Zayd was struck by a stray arrow while setting the Prophet's saddle; the Prophet said the stolen cloak he wore would burn him in Hell, and another man admitted taking two sandal straps and received the same warning.
[AKHFASH:v2p404/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | reports | Arabic has both qadr and qadar in expressions such as qadr/qadar shibr and qadartu aqdiru qadran; both vowelings also occur in the saying al-qadr.
[AKHFASH:v2p404/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The phrase is elliptical: from what they kindle for ornament or use comes foam like this foam.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p227/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The valleys flow according to their own capacities, whether small or large.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p227/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Rābiyan describes foam rising high above the water.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p227/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Ḥilyah means ornaments or jewelry.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p227/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Matāʿ means utensils; smelted metals and minerals produce dross like water produces foam.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p227/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Jufāʾ is what a valley casts onto its banks; ajfaʾat a pot means it cast off its foam.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p196/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The water and metal similes teach that falsehood may temporarily rise over truth but God will erase it and give the final outcome to truth and its people.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p196/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | A generous rain fills each valley according to its capacity: the large receives much and the small receives little.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p196/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The foam that rises above floodwater represents how falsehood sometimes appears to prevail over truth; smelted metals likewise produce dross.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p196/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The metals are gold and silver for jewelry and copper and iron for tools; their smelting produces foam like that on water.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p196/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Water casts foam onto tree roots and valley sides, and a furnace casts off metal impurities; the useful water and pure metal remain, representing truth.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p275#2/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | متاع can mean a period of time, as in the statements that people have enjoyment on earth until a term and that it may be a trial and enjoyment for a term. | mentions 2:36, 21:111
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p275#2/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | In 13:17, متاع means useful implements or articles.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p275#2/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | متاع also means benefit or usefulness, as in provisions for people and livestock, sea food for travelers, and empty houses that shelter visitors from heat and cold; it also underlies the divorced woman’s mutʿa. | mentions 56:73, 79:33, 5:96, 24:29
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p49/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas describes Paradise’s date palms as having emerald trunks, red-gold branches, leaves that become clothing, and fruit larger than jars and buckets, white as milk, sweeter than honey, softer than butter, and seedless.
[TAB-FULL:v13p496/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The two parables compare truth and falsehood, and faith and disbelief: truth remains beneficial while falsehood vanishes.
[TAB-FULL:v13p496/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The valleys carry water according to their capacities, the larger carrying more and the smaller less; the water represents truth and its rising foam falsehood.
[TAB-FULL:v13p496/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | A second parable is metal fired to obtain gold or silver ornaments and useful goods such as copper, lead, and iron; dross is falsehood and the useful pure metal remains.
[TAB-FULL:v13p496/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The foam on floodwater and the dross of fired metals are carried off by wind or water, thrown against trees and valley sides, and become useless.
[TAB-FULL:v13p496/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The noun al-zabad is nominative under the construction “and among what they fire in the furnace is foam,” with the implied comparison to flood foam.
[TAB-FULL:v13p499/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas compares hearts receiving the parable to valleys receiving water according to their certainty or doubt: doubt does not benefit, while certainty does; foam is doubt and lasting water is certainty.
[TAB-FULL:v13p499/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas says the flood carries wood and manure, while useful water and purified metals illustrate good deeds, guidance, and truth that endure; on Judgment Day falsehood disappears and the people of truth benefit.
[TAB-FULL:v13p499/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan explains ornaments as gold and silver and useful goods as copper and iron; firing removes impurity, just as truth remains for its adherents to benefit from.
[TAB-FULL:v13p500/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says each valley holds as much as it can; metal goods include iron, copper, and lead, whose dross resembles flood foam, and the water and foam represent truth and falsehood.
[TAB-FULL:v13p500/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj glosses the foam's going as its freezing on the ground, and says the water that remains is the beneficial element; both images represent truth and falsehood.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عوف | reports | A report reaching ʿAwf says valleys carry water by their size; foam is scattered by wind, while pure water remains for drink, crops, and use, and useful purified metal remains as well.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd applies the parable to truth and falsehood: foam and dross are useless, while water and sound jewelry remain and benefit people.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas says the small valley carries according to its small size and the large valley according to its large size.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عطاء | reports | ʿAṭāʾ says truth is like the floodwater that stays in the earth, while falsehood is like foam that does not benefit people.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Rābiyan means high or swollen, from rabā/yurbi; rābiya also names a raised mound, and 22:5 uses the same root for the earth swelling. | mentions 22:5
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#2/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The metals are called matāʿ because people make use of them; matāʿ broadly means anything people enjoy, as the poet's line about what remains before death illustrates.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#3/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlā says a pot “jafaʾa” when, as it boils, its foam pours out, or when it settles and no foam remains.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#3/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض أهل العربية من أهل البصرة | reports | Some Basran grammarians say the foam is absorbed by the earth; they connect jafā and ajfā to drying, while injafā describes a valley bringing down flood debris.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#3/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · العرب | reports | Arabic usage says jafaʾtu the pot means to pour out its foam, ajfaʾtuhu is another form, and jafaʾtu a man means to knock him down.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503#3/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قيل | reports | One analysis treats jufāʾ as jufʾan, a verbal noun used as a noun; Arabic similarly uses forms such as qumāsh, duqāq, huṭām, and ghuthāʾ as nouns.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says each valley carries water according to its size and the foam rises high; he describes three examples in one parable, with vanishing foam as falsehood and enduring water and refined metal as truth.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada explains al-jufāʾ as matter that clings to trees; the foam becomes useless and loses any hoped-for blessing, like falsehood.
[TAB-FULL:v13p503/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada identifies useful goods as iron and ṣufr (copper/brass); after its dross is removed, the useful metal remains, just as truth remains for its people.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p144/r10] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The segment begins to compare the believer, his belief, and faith's benefit to the water in the parable.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p144/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The command to declare God creator of everything is supported by the surah's earlier evidence for His oneness, then leads into a parable about believers and unbelievers. | mentions 13:17
[ZAJJAJ:v3p144/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The valleys flowed according to the amount God had allotted them to hold; alternatively, the phrase means according to their capacity.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p144/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The foam is floating high above the water.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p144/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The phrase means kindling material in pursuit of useful goods.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p144/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Gold and silver are heated for jewelry; iron, brass, copper, and lead are heated to make useful articles.

[ZAJJAJ:v3p144/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Foam includes water froth and the dross of iron, brass, copper, and lead; it goes away uselessly, cast up by the valley.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p144/r9] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The beneficial water, silver, gold, iron, and other materials listed remain in the earth.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p83/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Ibn Mujahid gives a transmission route for Abu Amr's reading through Mujahid, Ibn Abbas, and Ubayy back to the Prophet.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p83/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abu Amr names Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Ibn Kathir, and Hamid ibn Qays among those from whom he read.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p83/r3] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Sa'id ibn Jubayr heard Abu Amr's recitation and told him to adhere to it.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p83/r4] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abu Amr is reported as saying that he took readings from Nasr ibn Asim and his associates.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p83/r5] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | rejects | Abu Amr rejects that attribution, saying he took his readings from the people of the Hijaz, not Nasr ibn Asim and his companions.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p83/r6] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Ibn Mujahid describes Abu Amr's reading as well-chosen, easy, unforced, and inclined to lighten pronunciation where possible.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p83/r7] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Other eloquent Basran readers included Ibn Abi Ishaq, Asim al-Jahdari, and Isa ibn Umar, but their readings were less preserved and most Basrans adopted Abu Amr's.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p83/r8] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Abu Amr died in Kufa at Muhammad ibn Sulayman's; Waki reports reciting at his grave there.
[NAHHAS:v2p355/r4] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أهل التفسير | reports | Commentators explain بقدرها as either filling the valleys to capacity or the amount measured out for each.
[NAHHAS:v2p355/r5] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The flood clause is complete; Basran grammarians parse زبد as the subject in the next sentence.
[NAHHAS:v2p355/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisa'i parses زبد as raised because the sense is “from what you heat over fire, there is scum”; it is useless froth like sea foam.
[NAHHAS:v2p355/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | كذلك is accusative.
[NAHHAS:v2p355/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | جفاء is circumstantial and comes from انجفأت القدر when a pot casts away its froth; it also means dross.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p201/r2] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | reports | “Mimmā yūqidūna ʿalayhi” likewise varies between tāʾ and yāʾ, with the rationale given earlier.
[BAQILLANI:v1p143/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | reports | A letter sent to ʿAlī during the siege says the crisis has reached its limit and urges him to come to the sender’s aid, ending with a plea to rescue the sender before being torn apart.
[BAQILLANI:v1p181/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The poem is good but not extraordinarily accomplished; it shows some affectation and artifice.
[BAQILLANI:v1p181/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | “The fetter of wild beasts” is a fine but common conceit, easy to imitate; later poets deliberately compose such devices, whereas earlier masters produced them naturally.
[BAQILLANI:v1p181/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | “Twisting, charging, advancing, retreating” combines antithesis and simile, but poets describe a horse’s speed more delicately elsewhere.
[BAQILLANI:v1p181/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The line’s four comparisons are artful but have been rivaled, and the device is readily achieved.
[BAQILLANI:v1p181/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Poems fluctuate between excellence and weakness, ease and strain; by contrast, the Qurʾānic model maintains an ordered, clear, consistent composition through all its modes.
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · أصحابنا | reports | The majority of Bāqillānī’s Ashʿarite companions, including Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, hold that at least a complete sura, or an equal amount, is inimitable.
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r10] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · بعض الكبراء | reports | A senior authority suggests that the status of each passage as miraculous could instead be known through authoritative designation.
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r11] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | prefers | Bāqillānī prefers the argument from Arab incapacity, while allowing that multiple routes to knowledge of inimitability may converge.
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r12] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The first method shows that the same basis for the Qurʾān’s inimitability exists in every sura, short or long, so the judgment applies uniformly.
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · أبو الحسن الأشعري | reports | On this view, even a passage the length of the short sura al-Kawthar is miraculous; no proof establishes failure to match anything smaller.
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazila hold that every sura is independently miraculous.
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · بعضهم | reports | Some Muʿtazilites are reported to agree broadly with the Ashʿarites but require many verses, not a passage as long as a sura.
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Because the challenge covered all suras without exception and the Arabs matched none, every sura is shown to be inimitable.
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The challenge to produce a discourse like it does not conflict with the Ashʿarite minimum: a complete discourse cannot fit into fewer words than a short sura. | mentions 52:34
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r7] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | reports | Alternatively, “a discourse like it” can be read as a challenge to the class or kind of discourse, rather than each individual instance. | mentions 52:34
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r8] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The challenge to humans and jinn refers to the Qurʾān collectively; the proof does not depend on their failing to reproduce the entire book from beginning to end. | mentions 17:88
[BAQILLANI:v1p254/r9] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · أبو الحسن الأشعري | reports | Asked how one knows each short or long sura is miraculous, al-Ashʿarī answers that the Arabs’ inability to match each one establishes it.
[SULAMI:v1p330#3/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | God's pure pearl melted from shyness beneath His gaze of beauty; the flowing water signifies hearts purified and secrets made shy by that heavenly influx.
[SULAMI:v1p330#3/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | As a flood sweeps filth from valleys, God's allotted light flowing into hearts removes heedlessness and darkness; water is the light apportioned eternally, and valleys are hearts.
[SULAMI:v1p330#3/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Water represents kinds of divine gifts received according to each heart's share: guidance brings gnosis, love brings longing, and longing opens intimacy until hearts are immersed in witnessing.
[SULAMI:v1p330#3/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Truthful spiritual states leave their blessings fixed in hearts; states lacking truth retain no good.
[SULAMI:v1p330#3/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | Water is the Quran as divine generosity; foam is pride in one's deeds before companions, which vanishes for people of tawhid, while the lasting benefit is certainty granted by God.
[THALABI:v5p282#2/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The rain and smelting images are two parables illustrating truth and falsehood.
[THALABI:v5p282#2/r14] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Rain fills streams according to their capacity; the flood carries rising foam, while clear, useful water remains as the truth and disappearing debris is falsehood.
[THALABI:v5p282#2/r15] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Another view says the rain is the Qurʾān descending from heaven, with hearts receiving according to their measure of certainty or doubt, reason or ignorance; this too figures truth and falsehood.
[THALABI:v5p282#2/r16] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The commentary begins a second image: material heated in fire for ornament or useful goods produces foam like the flood's foam.
[THALABI:v5p283/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · حميد وأبو محجن وأبو وهب وحمزة والكسائي | reports | Hamid, Abu Mihjan, Abu Wahb, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read يوقدون with yāʾ.
[THALABI:v5p283/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Arab usage says the wind jafaʾa the clouds when it dispersed and carried them away.
[THALABI:v5p283/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · بعضهم | reports | Some explain the word as separation from the earth; a valley is said to jafaʾa when it dries up.
[THALABI:v5p283/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ treats jufāʾ as a verbal noun used like a concrete noun, as Arabs do with collective terms.
[THALABI:v5p283/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | What benefits people remains in the earth, while the flood's foam quickly disperses; this is an example of truth and falsehood.
[THALABI:v5p283/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عبيد | prefers | Abu Ubayd prefers the yāʾ reading because the verse says the useful things benefit people and does not address anyone directly.
[THALABI:v5p283/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Ḥilya means adornment made for wearing; matāʿ means something useful or anything one enjoys.
[THALABI:v5p283/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · المشعث | reports | Al-Mushaʿth's verse uses matāʿ for earthly valuables, identified as gold and silver.
[THALABI:v5p283/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Iron, brass, copper, and lead are heated to extract useful goods such as jewelry and vessels.
[THALABI:v5p283/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Like flood foam, smelting foam rises above pure useful metal; its impurity disappears, while useless foam resembles falsehood.
[THALABI:v5p283/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abu ʿAmr explains jufāʾ through pot foam spilling away when it boils or settling until no
